patterns.name: Arrays & Hashing
patterns.mantra: "Have I seen this before?" Ask the hash map, not the array.

patterns.name: Prefix Sum & Kadane
patterns.mantra: Keep a running total. A range sum is just two readings subtracted.

patterns.name: Sliding Window
patterns.mantra: Expand right. While it breaks the rule, shrink left.

patterns.name: Stack & Monotonic Stack
patterns.mantra: Last in, first out. A newcomer answers everyone smaller waiting below.

patterns.name: Binary Search
patterns.mantra: Halve the space. If you can check an answer, you can search for it.

patterns.name: Linked List
patterns.mantra: A dummy head plus fast and slow pointers solve most of them.

patterns.name: Trees
patterns.mantra: Trust the recursion: get answers from children, combine, return.

patterns.name: Heap / Priority Queue
patterns.mantra: Always need the smallest or largest next? Let the heap keep score.

patterns.name: Intervals
patterns.mantra: Sort first. By start to merge, by end to keep the most.

patterns.name: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Topo
patterns.mantra: Fewest steps → BFS. Weighted → Dijkstra. Prerequisites → topological sort.

patterns.name: Dynamic Programming
patterns.mantra: Recursion that keeps repeating itself? Write each answer in the notebook once.

patterns.name: Greedy
patterns.mantra: Take the locally best step, and be ready to say why it is safe.

patterns.name: Trie
patterns.mantra: Words that share a prefix share a road.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.story: Every number walks into a locker room and shouts: "Is my partner (target − me) already inside?"
problems.statement: Given an array and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Exactly one answer exists.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every pair (i, j)
if nums[i] + nums[j] == target → return {i, j}

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: store (value, index) pairs, sort by value
two pointers: sum too small → l++, too big → r--
solutions.intuition: After sorting, the smallest + largest pair tells you which way to move: too big means the largest can never be used with anything bigger, so drop it; too small means drop the smallest. Each step throws away one number for good.
solutions.remember: Sort, then squeeze: big sum → drop the biggest, small sum → drop the smallest.

solutions.label: Best
steps: one pass: is (target − x) already in the map? → answer
otherwise store x → index
solutions.intuition: For every x you already know exactly which partner you need: target − x. The naive loop searches for it; a hash map just remembers everything seen so far, so the search becomes a single O(1) lookup.
solutions.remember: Don't search for the partner, remember it: seen[target − x].

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.story: Two bags of Scrabble tiles — do they hold exactly the same tiles? Just count them.
problems.statement: Return true if t uses exactly the same letters as s, the same number of times.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: sort both strings
equal after sorting → anagram

solutions.label: Best
steps: one count[26]: +1 for s, −1 for t
all zeros → anagram
solutions.intuition: Order does not matter for an anagram, only how many of each letter. Counting 26 letters is cheaper than sorting, and +1 for s / −1 for t means a perfect match leaves every counter at zero.
solutions.remember: Anagram = same letter counts → one count array, +s −t, all zeros.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.story: Sort a word's letters and it becomes its family surname ("eat" → "aet"). Same surname → same house.
problems.statement: Group the words that are anagrams of each other. Any order is fine.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: for each unused word, compare it with every later word
sorted-equal → same group

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: key = sorted word
map[key].push_back(word)
solutions.intuition: All anagrams look identical once their letters are sorted, so the sorted word is a perfect group ID. Instead of comparing words pairwise, drop each word into the bucket of its ID.
solutions.remember: Sorted word = family surname → hash map of surname → words.

solutions.label: Best
steps: key = 26 letter counts (no sorting)
map[key].push_back(word)
solutions.intuition: Sorting each word costs k log k. The 26 letter counts identify the family just as well and take O(k) to build, so use the count signature as the key instead.
solutions.remember: Same counts, same family: the key is the 26 counts, no sorting.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.story: Election night: count the votes, then put each candidate on the shelf numbered by their vote count. Read shelves from the top.
problems.statement: Return the k numbers that appear most often.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: count frequencies
sort (freq, value) descending, take first k

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: count frequencies
min-heap of size k: push, pop when size > k
solutions.intuition: You only care about the k best, so never keep more than k. A min-heap of size k keeps the weakest of the current top k on top; anything weaker than it can be thrown out immediately.
solutions.remember: Top k → min-heap of size k, kick out the weakest.

solutions.label: Best
steps: bucket[freq] = list of numbers (freq ≤ n)
walk buckets from n down, collect k
solutions.intuition: A frequency can never exceed n, so frequencies are small whole numbers. Put each number on the shelf of its frequency and read shelves from the top: no comparison sort needed.
solutions.remember: Frequency ≤ n → bucket by frequency, read from the top shelf.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.story: Each person's gift = product of everyone on their LEFT × everyone on their RIGHT. One sunrise pass, one sunset pass.
problems.statement: Return an array where each position holds the product of every other element, without using division.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: for each i multiply every j ≠ i

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: pre[i] = product of everything left of i
suf[i] = product of everything right of i; answer = pre × suf
solutions.intuition: "Everything except me" = everything on my left × everything on my right. Both sides are running products you can build in one pass each, so no division and no repeated multiplying.
solutions.remember: Except-self = left product × right product.

solutions.label: Best
steps: write prefix products into the answer
sweep back with a running suffix variable
solutions.intuition: The left products can live in the answer array itself, and the right product only needs one running variable while you walk back. Same idea as two arrays, minus the extra memory.
solutions.remember: Left pass fills the answer, right pass multiplies in a running suffix.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.story: Only the FIRST domino of a chain (nobody at x−1) starts counting how far the chain falls.
problems.statement: Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array, in O(n).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: for each x, keep looking for x+1, x+2… with a linear search

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: sort; skip duplicates
+1 neighbour extends the run, else reset
solutions.intuition: Sorting puts every consecutive chain side by side, so one left-to-right walk can count chain lengths. Duplicates are skipped because they neither break nor extend a chain.
solutions.remember: Sort, then count runs where next = prev + 1.

solutions.label: Best
steps: put everything in a hash set
start counting only where x−1 is missing (chain head)
solutions.intuition: A chain only needs to be counted once, from its first number. A number is a chain head exactly when x − 1 is missing from the set, so start counting only there; every number is visited at most twice overall.
solutions.remember: Only the first domino (no x − 1) starts counting.

problems.title: Least Number of Unique Integers after K Removals
problems.story: You have k bullets. Shoot the SMALLEST gangs first — every gang wiped out is one less unique number.
problems.statement: Remove exactly k elements so that as few distinct numbers as possible remain. Return how many remain.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: count frequencies
k times: find the least-frequent number, remove one copy

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: collect frequencies, sort ascending
while k ≥ freq: k −= freq, unique−−
solutions.intuition: Each removal should finish off a whole distinct number as cheaply as possible. The cheapest numbers to eliminate are the rarest ones, so sort the frequencies and spend k on the smallest first.
solutions.remember: Kill the smallest gangs first.

solutions.label: Best
steps: cntOfFreq[f] = how many numbers appear f times
for f = 1..n remove as many whole groups as k allows
solutions.intuition: You only need frequencies in increasing order, and frequencies are at most n. Counting how many numbers have each frequency gives that order without sorting.
solutions.remember: Counting sort on frequencies: walk sizes 1, 2, 3 … and spend k.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.story: Kadane's bank balance: the moment your running balance goes negative, tear up the passbook and start fresh.
problems.statement: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every start i, extend j and keep a running sum

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: prefix sums: best = pre[i] − smallest earlier prefix
solutions.intuition: A subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums. For each end point, the best start is the one with the smallest prefix before it, so track the running minimum prefix.
solutions.remember: Best subarray ending here = prefix now − smallest earlier prefix.

solutions.label: Best
steps: cur = max(x, cur + x)  (restart or extend)
best = max(best, cur)
solutions.intuition: If the sum carried in from the left is negative, it can only drag you down, so it is better to start fresh at the current number. Otherwise keep extending. The best value ever seen is the answer.
solutions.remember: Negative balance? Tear up the passbook and start fresh.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.story: Odometer trick: if it reads P now and read P − k earlier, the stretch in between was exactly k km.
problems.statement: Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k (numbers can be negative).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every start i, extend j, count sums equal to k

solutions.label: Best
steps: running prefix sum; map counts of earlier prefixes (start with {0:1})
answer += count[prefix − k]
solutions.intuition: A subarray (i, j] sums to k exactly when prefix[j] − prefix[i] = k, i.e. an earlier prefix equals prefix[j] − k. Counting earlier prefixes in a map answers "how many such i" in O(1) per position. Seed the map with {0: 1} for subarrays starting at index 0.
solutions.remember: Count of earlier prefixes equal to (now − k); seed with prefix 0.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.story: Walk through the days remembering the cheapest day so far; every day ask "what if I sold today?"
problems.statement: prices[i] is the price on day i. Buy once and sell once on a later day; return the maximum profit (0 if none).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every buy day i and sell day j > i

solutions.label: Best
steps: track min price so far
profit today = price − min
solutions.intuition: For a sell day, the best buy day is simply the cheapest day before it. Keep that minimum as you walk, and every day check "what if I sold today?".
solutions.remember: Remember the cheapest day so far; sell today and compare.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.story: Two friends start at opposite ends of a bridge and walk toward each other, hopping over puddles (non-letters). They must see the same letter at every step.
problems.statement: After lowercasing and removing everything except letters and digits, does the string read the same both ways?
problems.example: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true

solutions.label: Naive
steps: build a cleaned lowercase string
compare it with its reverse

solutions.label: Best
steps: l from left, r from right, skip non-alphanumerics
mismatch → false
solutions.intuition: A palindrome compares the i-th character from the left with the i-th from the right. Walk two pointers inward, skipping non-alphanumerics, instead of building a cleaned copy.
solutions.remember: Two friends walk inward, skip puddles, must match every step.

problems.title: Two Sum II – Input Array Is Sorted
problems.story: A sorted array is a seesaw: sum too heavy → right friend steps in; too light → left friend steps in.
problems.statement: The array is sorted. Return the 1-indexed positions of two numbers that add up to target, using O(1) extra space.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every pair

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: for each i, binary-search target − numbers[i] to its right
solutions.intuition: The array is sorted, so for each number the partner target − x can be found with binary search instead of a scan.
solutions.remember: Sorted → binary-search the partner.

solutions.label: Best
steps: sum < target → l++; sum > target → r--
solutions.intuition: Sorted order gives you direction: if l + r is too big, r can never pair with anything (everything else is ≥ l), so move r left; too small, move l right. One pass, no extra memory.
solutions.remember: Seesaw: too heavy → r−−, too light → l++.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.story: Pick a captain, then run the Two-Sum seesaw on the players to his right. Skip twins so you never form the same team twice.
problems.statement: Return every unique triplet that sums to 0.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try all triples, sort each, dedupe with a set

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: fix i; for j > i look up −(a[i]+a[j]) in a hash set
solutions.intuition: Fix the first number; now you need two others summing to −a[i], which is Two Sum. A hash set of numbers seen between i and j finds the third in O(1); a set of triplets removes duplicates.
solutions.remember: 3Sum = fix one + Two Sum with a hash set.

solutions.label: Best
steps: sort; for each captain i (skip duplicates)
two pointers l, r on the rest; skip duplicates after a hit
solutions.intuition: Sort once, fix a captain, and run the two-pointer Two Sum on the rest. Sorting also makes duplicates neighbours, so skipping equal values gives unique triplets without a set.
solutions.remember: Sort, fix i, squeeze l and r, skip twins.

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.story: The water level is set by the SHORTER wall. Moving the taller wall can never help, so always move the short one.
problems.statement: Each value is a vertical wall. Pick the two walls that hold the most water between them.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every pair of walls

solutions.label: Best
steps: l = 0, r = n−1, area = width × shorter wall
move the pointer at the shorter wall inward
solutions.intuition: Area is limited by the shorter wall. Moving the taller wall inward can only shrink the width and never raise the limit, so the only move that can help is moving the shorter wall.
solutions.remember: Always move the shorter wall.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.story: Each bar holds water = min(tallest wall on its left, tallest on its right) − its own height.
problems.statement: Given bar heights, how much rain water is trapped between the bars?

solutions.label: Naive
steps: for every bar scan left max and right max

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: precompute leftMax[] and rightMax[] arrays
solutions.intuition: Water above a bar = min(tallest on its left, tallest on its right) − its height. Those two maxima can be precomputed for every index in two passes, instead of rescanning for each bar.
solutions.remember: Precompute leftMax[] and rightMax[], then min − height.

solutions.label: Best
steps: two pointers; the side with the smaller wall is "settled"
add (sideMax − height) on that side, move it inward
solutions.intuition: If the left wall is lower than the right wall, the water at l is decided only by leftMax, because something at least as tall is guaranteed on the right. So settle the lower side, add its water and move it inward.
solutions.remember: The lower side is settled: add water there, move it in.

problems.title: Sort Colors
problems.story: Dutch flag: red gets pushed to the left wall, blue to the right wall, white stays in the middle. One sweeper walks through.
problems.statement: Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in place, in one pass, without a library sort.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: just sort

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: count 0s, 1s, 2s; rewrite the array
solutions.intuition: There are only three possible values, so counting how many of each and rewriting the array is enough.
solutions.remember: Only 3 colours → count, then rewrite.

solutions.label: Best
steps: lo = next slot for 0, hi = next slot for 2, mid = sweeper
0 → swap with lo; 2 → swap with hi (don't advance mid); 1 → mid++
solutions.intuition: Keep three zones: 0s before lo, 2s after hi, 1s between lo and mid. Each element is looked at once and swapped straight into its zone. After swapping with hi, re-check mid because the incoming value is unknown.
solutions.remember: 0 → swap left, 1 → step, 2 → swap right (don't step).

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.story: A train window sliding over letters: the moment a duplicate passenger boards, kick people out from the back until everyone is unique again.
problems.statement: Find the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every start i, extend j until a repeat

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: window [l, r] kept in a set
while s[r] is already inside, erase s[l++]
solutions.intuition: Valid windows only grow on the right and shrink on the left. When a duplicate enters, drop characters from the left until it is gone; each character enters and leaves the set once.
solutions.remember: Window with a set: duplicate boards → evict from the back.

solutions.label: Best
steps: remember last index of each char
on a repeat inside the window, jump l to last+1 directly
solutions.intuition: Instead of evicting one by one, remember where each character was last seen. If that position is inside the window, jump l straight past it.
solutions.remember: Store last index; on a repeat jump l to last + 1.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.story: A window is fine if (window size − count of its most common letter) ≤ k paint strokes. Too many strokes needed → shrink from the left.
problems.statement: You may change up to k characters. Return the length of the longest substring that can become a single repeated letter.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every start i, extend j, track max letter count

solutions.label: Best
steps: expand r, update maxCount
while (len − maxCount > k) shrink l
solutions.intuition: A window can be made all one letter if (length − count of its most common letter) ≤ k. Grow the window; when it needs too many repaints, slide the left edge. The best window length seen is the answer.
solutions.remember: Valid if len − maxCount ≤ k; otherwise shrink.

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.story: Slide a stencil the size of s1 across s2. When the letters under the stencil have the same counts as s1, you found it.
problems.statement: Does s2 contain some rearrangement of s1 as a contiguous substring?

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every window of size m: sort and compare with sorted s1

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: count arrays for s1 and the current window
slide: add right char, remove left char, compare arrays
solutions.intuition: A permutation of s1 is any window of the same length with the same letter counts. Slide a fixed-size window and update counts incrementally: one letter in, one letter out.
solutions.remember: Fixed window of |s1|, compare 26 counts while sliding.

solutions.label: Best
steps: need[] = counts still missing; missing = m
add char: if it was needed, missing−−; drop char: if now needed, missing++
solutions.intuition: Track how many letters are still missing instead of comparing 26 counts each time. Entering letters that were needed reduce it; leaving letters that become needed increase it. Missing = 0 means a match.
solutions.remember: Keep a "missing" counter; zero means found.

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.story: Shopping-cart window: push right until the cart holds the whole list, then pop from the left while it still does. Keep the smallest cart.
problems.statement: Find the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t (counting duplicates).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every start i: extend j until all of t is covered

solutions.label: Best
steps: expand r: if s[r] was needed, missing−−
while missing == 0: record, then drop s[l++] (missing++ if it becomes needed)
solutions.intuition: Expand right until the window covers everything in t, then shrink from the left as long as it still covers t. Every valid window is visited, each pointer moves at most n times, and the smallest is kept.
solutions.remember: Expand until it has everything, shrink while it still does.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.story: The bouncer's queue: a tall newcomer throws out everyone shorter standing behind him, since they can never be the tallest again. The front of the queue is the current king.
problems.statement: For every window of size k sliding across the array, report its maximum.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: for every window scan its max

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: keep the window in a multiset (sorted)
add new, erase the one leaving, max = last element
solutions.intuition: Keep the window in a sorted multiset so the maximum is always the last element. Each step inserts one value and erases one, both O(log k).
solutions.remember: Sorted window: insert new, erase old, max = last.

solutions.label: Best
steps: deque of indices with decreasing values
drop front if it left the window; pop back while smaller than new
solutions.intuition: A smaller number to the left of a bigger one can never be the max again while the bigger one is in the window. Keep a deque of candidates in decreasing order: pop smaller ones from the back, expired ones from the front.
solutions.remember: Tall newcomer kicks out shorter ones; front is the king.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.story: A stack of plates: every opener puts a plate on top; every closer must match the TOP plate exactly or the tower falls.
problems.statement: Is a string of ( ) [ ] { } brackets opened and closed correctly, in the right order?

solutions.label: Naive
steps: keep deleting "()", "[]", "{}" until nothing changes
empty at the end → valid

solutions.label: Best
steps: opener → push
closer → stack top must be its partner, pop
solutions.intuition: The most recently opened bracket must close first, which is exactly last-in-first-out. Push openers; each closer must match the top.
solutions.remember: Last opened, first closed → stack.

problems.title: Min Stack
problems.story: Every plate carries a sticky note saying "smallest plate at or below me". When you pop the plate, its note leaves with it.
problems.statement: Design a stack with push, pop, top and getMin, all in O(1).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: plain stack; scan for min when asked

solutions.label: Best
steps: push (value, min(value, previous min))
solutions.intuition: The minimum only changes when you push or pop, so record "the min at or below me" with every element. When it is popped, the previous min is already stored underneath.
solutions.remember: Every plate carries a note: min so far.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.story: A calculator built on a plate pile: numbers go on the pile; an operator eats the top two plates and puts the result back.
problems.statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression written in Reverse Polish Notation (operators come after their operands).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: find the first operator, combine the two numbers before it
splice the result back, repeat

solutions.label: Best
steps: number → push
operator → pop b, pop a, push a op b
solutions.intuition: In postfix, an operator always applies to the two most recent values, which are on top of a stack. Pop two, apply, push the result.
solutions.remember: Numbers pile up; an operator eats the top two.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.story: Cold days wait in a line (stack). When a warm day arrives, every colder day still waiting gets its answer and leaves the line.
problems.statement: For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature? Use 0 if it never gets warmer.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: for each day scan forward for the first warmer day

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: monotonic stack of indices (decreasing temps)
warmer day pops all colder ones and fills their answers
solutions.intuition: A day waits on the stack until a warmer day shows up. When it does, every colder waiting day gets its answer at once. Each day is pushed and popped once.
solutions.remember: Colder days wait on a stack; a warm day answers them.

solutions.label: Best
steps: go right-to-left; hop using answers already computed
j += res[j] skips days that are known to be colder
solutions.intuition: Going right to left, answers to the right are already known. If day j is not warmer, jump by its answer res[j] straight to the next day warmer than j, skipping everything in between.
solutions.remember: Hop using answers you already have.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problems.story: Each bar asks: "How far can I stretch left and right before I hit someone shorter?" Width × my height = my rectangle.
problems.statement: Find the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside a histogram.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every start i, extend j, keep min height

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: prev-smaller index L[i] and next-smaller index R[i] via stacks
area = h[i] × (R[i] − L[i] − 1)
solutions.intuition: The best rectangle using bar i as its height stretches until the first shorter bar on each side. Monotonic stacks find "previous shorter" and "next shorter" for every bar in O(n).
solutions.remember: Height × (nextSmaller − prevSmaller − 1).

solutions.label: Best
steps: increasing stack; a shorter bar (or the 0 sentinel at the end) pops taller bars
popped bar's width = i − (new top) − 1
solutions.intuition: Keep bars in increasing height on a stack. When a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar it pops now knows both boundaries: the new bar on the right and the bar below it on the left.
solutions.remember: A shorter bar pops taller ones and closes their rectangles.

problems.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
problems.story: The stack remembers where the last "wall" is (an unmatched ')' or the −1 floor). Every match measures its distance back to that wall.
problems.statement: Return the length of the longest substring of well-formed parentheses.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: every start i: balance counter; < 0 break; == 0 record length

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: stack of indices, start with −1
'(' push i; ')' pop → empty? push i (new wall) : len = i − top
solutions.intuition: Keep the index of the last position that cannot be part of a valid run (start with −1) at the bottom of the stack. Every ")" that finds a match measures its length back to that wall; an unmatched ")" becomes the new wall.
solutions.remember: Stack holds the last wall; length = i − wall.

solutions.label: Best
steps: left→right: count open/close; equal → record; close > open → reset
right→left: same with roles swapped (catches "(()")
solutions.intuition: Count opens and closes left to right: equal means a valid run, more closes means it is broken, so reset. Runs like "(()" never balance this way, so repeat the scan right to left with the roles swapped.
solutions.remember: Two passes of counters: reset when it breaks.

problems.title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
problems.story: A bouncer with a guest list: an unmatched ')' is thrown out on the spot; '(' still waiting on the stack are thrown out at closing time.
problems.statement: Remove the fewest parentheses so the string becomes valid. Letters stay as they are.

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: stack of '(' indices; ')' with empty stack → mark drop
leftover stack indices → mark drop; rebuild string
solutions.intuition: A ")" with no "(" before it can never be matched, so drop it immediately. A "(" still waiting at the end was never closed, so drop those too. Track waiting "(" positions on a stack.
solutions.remember: Unmatched ) now, unmatched ( at the end.

solutions.label: Best
steps: pass 1 (left→right): skip ')' with no open '('
pass 2 (right→left): skip the extra '(' still open
solutions.intuition: Same rule as the stack, using counts: the first pass drops ")" that arrive with nothing open; the open count left over is exactly how many "(" to drop, taken from the right end.
solutions.remember: Left pass drops bad ), right pass drops extra (.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.story: Open the dictionary in the middle. Wrong half? Tear it off. Every guess halves the book.
problems.statement: Find target in a sorted array in O(log n); return its index or −1.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: scan left to right

solutions.label: Best
steps: lo..hi; m = lo + (hi−lo)/2
too small → lo = m+1; too big → hi = m−1
solutions.intuition: In a sorted array, one comparison with the middle tells you which half cannot contain the target, so you can throw that half away. log n halvings reach a single element.
solutions.remember: Compare with mid, discard the wrong half.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.story: A rotated clock face: cut it anywhere and at least ONE half is still in order. Ask: does the target live inside the ordered half?
problems.statement: A sorted array was rotated at an unknown point. Find target in O(log n).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: linear scan

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: binary-search the pivot (smallest element)
normal binary search in the half that can contain target
solutions.intuition: A rotated array is two sorted runs. Binary-search the pivot (the smallest element) first, then do a normal binary search in the run that can contain the target.
solutions.remember: Find the pivot, then search the right run.

solutions.label: Best
steps: if left half sorted: target inside it? go left : go right
else right half sorted: target inside it? go right : go left
solutions.intuition: Cut a rotated array anywhere and at least one half is sorted. Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half; if yes go there, otherwise go to the other half.
solutions.remember: One half is always sorted: is the target inside it?

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.story: Compare the middle with the RIGHT end. If the middle is bigger, the cliff (minimum) is somewhere to the right.
problems.statement: Find the minimum of a rotated sorted array of distinct values in O(log n).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: min_element

solutions.label: Best
steps: nums[m] > nums[hi] → lo = m+1, else hi = m
solutions.intuition: Compare mid with the right end. If mid is bigger, the drop (minimum) must be to the right of mid; otherwise mid could be the minimum, so keep it and search left.
solutions.remember: mid > right end → the cliff is to the right.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.story: Binary search on the ANSWER: guess a speed and ask "can I finish in h hours?" Yes → try slower. No → speed up.
problems.statement: Koko eats from one pile per hour at k bananas per hour. Find the smallest k that finishes every pile within h hours.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try speeds 1, 2, 3… until total hours ≤ h

solutions.label: Best
steps: lo = 1, hi = max pile
feasible(mid) → hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1
solutions.intuition: If Koko can finish at speed k, she can finish at any speed above k: the yes/no answer flips only once. Binary-search that flip point between 1 and the largest pile.
solutions.remember: Binary search on the answer: smallest speed that works.

problems.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
problems.story: Truck-size guessing game: smallest possible truck = heaviest parcel, biggest = all parcels together. Binary-search the smallest truck that finishes in D days.
problems.statement: Ship packages in the given order within D days. Find the smallest truck capacity that makes it.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every capacity from max(w) up to sum(w)

solutions.label: Best
steps: binary search capacity in [max, sum]
ok(cap): greedily fill the truck, count days
solutions.intuition: A bigger truck never needs more days, so "can ship in D days" is monotonic in capacity. Binary-search the capacity between the heaviest parcel and the total weight, checking each guess greedily.
solutions.remember: Monotonic yes/no → binary search on capacity.

problems.title: Find Peak Element
problems.story: A hiker in fog: if the path goes UP to the right, a peak must exist on the right. Keep walking uphill, halving the trail each time.
problems.statement: Return the index of any element strictly greater than its neighbours, in O(log n).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: first i with nums[i] > nums[i+1] is a peak

solutions.label: Best
steps: nums[m] < nums[m+1] → uphill on right: lo = m+1, else hi = m
solutions.intuition: If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], the path goes up to the right, and an upward path must reach a peak before it ends. So a peak is guaranteed on that side; otherwise mid or something to its left is a peak.
solutions.remember: Walk uphill; a peak must be there.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.story: Train coaches: walk forward and flip each coupling to point backward. You need three hands: prev, cur, next.
problems.statement: Reverse a singly linked list.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: copy values to a vector, write them back reversed

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: reverse the rest, then make head->next point back to head
solutions.intuition: Trust the recursion: reverse everything after head, then the node right after head (now the tail of the reversed part) should point back to head, and head becomes the new tail.
solutions.remember: Reverse the rest, then hook head on at the end.

solutions.label: Best
steps: save next, flip cur->next = prev, step prev and cur forward
solutions.intuition: Walk once and flip each next pointer backward. Save next before flipping or you lose the rest of the list; prev ends up as the new head.
solutions.remember: Save next, flip, step prev and cur.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.story: A zipper: two sorted chains, always pull the smaller tooth next. A dummy head is your zipper pull.
problems.statement: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: dump all values, sort, build a new list

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: smaller head wins; its next = merge(rest)
solutions.intuition: The smaller of the two heads must come first. Its next is just the merge of everything that is left, which is the same problem again.
solutions.remember: Smaller head wins; its next = merge(rest).

solutions.label: Best
steps: dummy + tail pointer; attach the smaller node each step
attach whatever is left over
solutions.intuition: Like a zipper: keep a tail pointer and always attach the smaller front node. A dummy head removes the special case for the first node; leftovers are already sorted, so attach them as is.
solutions.remember: Dummy head + always pull the smaller tooth.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle
problems.story: Tortoise and hare on a race track: if the track is a loop, the fast hare eventually laps the slow tortoise.
problems.statement: Does the linked list contain a cycle? Use O(1) memory.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: remember every visited node in a hash set

solutions.label: Best
steps: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; they meet → cycle
solutions.intuition: On a loop, a runner moving 2 steps closes the gap to a runner moving 1 step by one node per move, so it must land on it. Without a loop the fast runner falls off the end.
solutions.remember: Tortoise and hare: they meet only on a loop.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.story: Two runners tied with an n-step rope. When the front runner crosses the finish line, the back runner is standing just before the victim.
problems.statement: Remove the n-th node from the end of the list, in one pass.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: count length L, walk L−n steps from a dummy, unlink next

solutions.label: Best
steps: move fast n+1 steps ahead from the dummy
move both until fast is null; unlink slow->next
solutions.intuition: Keep a gap of n + 1 nodes between two pointers. When the front one falls off the end, the back one is exactly one node before the one to delete. A dummy node handles deleting the head.
solutions.remember: Rope of n + 1 nodes: front hits null, back is just before the victim.

problems.title: LRU Cache
problems.story: A party line: whoever you talk to moves to the FRONT. When the room is full, the person at the very back (least recently talked to) leaves. The hash map is the guest list for O(1) lookup.
problems.statement: Design a fixed-capacity cache with O(1) get and put. When full, evict the least recently used key.
problems.example: cap 2: put 1, put 2, get 1, put 3 → key 2 is evicted

solutions.label: Naive
steps: vector of (key, value), front = most recent
linear search; move to front; pop back when over capacity

solutions.label: Best
steps: doubly linked list (order) + hash map key → list node
get/put: splice node to front; evict from back
solutions.intuition: You need O(1) lookup (hash map) and O(1) "move to front / remove from back" (doubly linked list). The map stores each key's node, so you can splice it to the front without searching.
solutions.remember: Hash map for finding, linked list for ordering.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.story: Ask each child "how tall are you?", take the taller answer and add 1 for yourself. Recursion is just delegating to your children.
problems.statement: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.

solutions.label: Recursive DFS
steps: depth = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)); null → 0
solutions.intuition: The depth of a tree is 1 (the root) plus the depth of its deeper subtree. An empty tree has depth 0. The recursion just asks each child and combines.
solutions.remember: Depth = 1 + max(left, right).

solutions.label: Iterative BFS
steps: process the queue one level at a time; count levels
solutions.intuition: Process the tree floor by floor with a queue; the number of floors you process is the depth.
solutions.remember: Count BFS levels.

problems.title: Invert Binary Tree
problems.story: Mirror selfie: at every node swap the left and right hands, then tell both children to do the same.
problems.statement: Mirror a binary tree: swap left and right children everywhere.

solutions.label: Recursive DFS
steps: swap(left, right), recurse on both
solutions.intuition: Mirroring a tree means swapping left and right at every node. Do it at the root, then let each child do the same for its own subtree.
solutions.remember: Swap my children, then recurse.

solutions.label: Iterative BFS
steps: queue; pop node, swap its children, push them
solutions.intuition: The order of swapping does not matter, only that every node gets swapped once, so a queue visiting every node works too.
solutions.remember: Visit every node once and swap its children.

problems.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
problems.story: The longest road through any town = deepest road going down-left + deepest road going down-right. Every node is a possible "bend" in the road.
problems.statement: Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: at every node: height(left) + height(right), recompute heights each time

solutions.label: Best
steps: one DFS returns height; on the way, best = max(best, L + R)
solutions.intuition: The longest path that bends at a node uses its left height + right height. A single DFS that returns heights can update the best bend on the way back up, instead of recomputing heights.
solutions.remember: Return height, update best with L + R.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.story: Floors of a building: before you start a floor, count how many people are in the queue (snapshot the size) and serve exactly that many.
problems.statement: Return the node values level by level, left to right.

solutions.label: DFS with depth
steps: dfs(node, depth): res[depth].push_back(val)
solutions.intuition: Carry the depth down the DFS and append each value to the list for its depth. Visiting left before right keeps each level in left-to-right order.
solutions.remember: res[depth].push_back(val).

solutions.label: BFS (standard)
steps: size = q.size(); pop size nodes into one level; push children
solutions.intuition: A queue serves nodes in the order they were discovered, which is level by level. Snapshot the queue size at the start of a level and pop exactly that many.
solutions.remember: Queue size at the start = nodes on this floor.

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.story: Every node carries a "permitted range" ticket handed down by its ancestors. Go left → the ceiling drops to me. Go right → the floor rises to me.
problems.statement: Is the tree a valid BST? Everything in a left subtree must be smaller, everything in a right subtree larger.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: in-order traversal into an array
must be strictly increasing

solutions.label: Best
steps: ok(node, lo, hi): lo < val < hi
left gets (lo, val), right gets (val, hi)
solutions.intuition: Every node must respect all of its ancestors, not just its parent. Pass down an allowed (low, high) range: going left lowers the ceiling to the node, going right raises the floor.
solutions.remember: Each node carries a range ticket from its ancestors.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
problems.story: Family reunion: each branch reports back "I found p" or "I found q". The first person who hears from BOTH sides is the common ancestor.
problems.statement: Find the lowest node that has both p and q below it (a node counts as below itself).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: find root→p path and root→q path
last common node on both paths

solutions.label: Best
steps: null or p or q → return it
both sides non-null → I am the LCA; else pass up the non-null side
solutions.intuition: Each subtree reports whether it contains p or q. The first node that hears from both its left and its right is the lowest node with both below it. If the node itself is p or q, it reports itself.
solutions.remember: First node with a hit on both sides is the LCA.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.story: An in-order walk of a BST reads the numbers in sorted order, like reading a bookshelf left to right. Stop at the k-th book.
problems.statement: Return the k-th smallest value in a BST.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: full in-order into a vector, return v[k−1]

solutions.label: Best
steps: iterative in-order with a stack
count down k as you pop; stop at 0
solutions.intuition: An in-order walk of a BST visits values in sorted order. Doing it iteratively lets you stop as soon as you have counted k nodes.
solutions.remember: In-order = sorted; stop at the k-th.

problems.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problems.story: Stand to the right of the building and look in: on each floor you only see the LAST person in that row.
problems.statement: Return the values you would see standing to the right of the tree, from top to bottom.

solutions.label: BFS
steps: level-order; record the last node of each level
solutions.intuition: From the right side you see the last node of every level. A level-order BFS hands you each level in order, so take its last node.
solutions.remember: Last node of each BFS level.

solutions.label: DFS right-first
steps: visit right before left; first node seen at each new depth is visible
solutions.intuition: If you always visit the right child first, the first node you reach at each new depth is the one visible from the right.
solutions.remember: Right-first DFS: first node at each new depth.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.story: A VIP lounge with only k seats and a bouncer who kicks out the weakest guest whenever it overflows. At closing time, the weakest VIP is the k-th largest.
problems.statement: Return the k-th largest element (counting duplicates).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: sort descending, return nums[k−1]

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: min-heap; push each; pop when size > k; top is the answer
solutions.intuition: Keep only the k largest seen so far in a min-heap. Its top is the smallest of those k, which is the k-th largest overall when you finish.
solutions.remember: Min-heap of size k; top = k-th largest.

solutions.label: Best
steps: quickselect: random pivot, 3-way partition
recurse only into the side that holds index n−k
solutions.intuition: Partitioning around a pivot puts it at its final sorted position. If that is not the target position n − k, you only need to continue on one side, which averages O(n).
solutions.remember: Quickselect: partition, keep only the side with the target.

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
problems.story: Keep a max-heap of your k nearest riders. When a closer rider shows up, the farthest of your k gets dropped.
problems.statement: Return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: sort by x² + y², take first k

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: max-heap of (dist, index), size ≤ k
solutions.intuition: Keep the k nearest in a max-heap by distance. The farthest of them sits on top, so any closer point replaces it.
solutions.remember: Max-heap of size k; drop the farthest.

solutions.label: Best
steps: quickselect (nth_element) by distance, take first k
solutions.intuition: You do not need the k points sorted, only separated from the rest. nth_element (quickselect) partitions around the k-th distance in average O(n).
solutions.remember: Partition around the k-th distance.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.story: k checkout counters, one exit door. A min-heap always tells you whose front customer walks out next.
problems.statement: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: collect every value, sort, build a list

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: push every list head into a min-heap
pop smallest, attach, push its next
solutions.intuition: The next node of the merged list is always the smallest among the current heads of the k lists. A min-heap gives that smallest head in O(log k).
solutions.remember: Heap of list heads; pop smallest, push its next.

solutions.label: Best
steps: divide & conquer: merge pairs (0,1),(2,3)… then (0,2)… like a tournament
solutions.intuition: Merging two sorted lists is easy. Merge them in pairs, then pairs of pairs, like a tournament: log k rounds, each touching all N nodes, with no heap.
solutions.remember: Pairwise merging, tournament style.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.story: The busiest task builds the skeleton: (maxFreq − 1) frames of width (n + 1), plus one slot for every task tied at the max. If the other tasks overflow the frames, there's no idle time.
problems.statement: Each task takes one unit; the same task needs n idle units between two runs. Return the minimum total time.

solutions.label: Simulation
steps: max-heap of remaining counts + cooldown queue (count, readyTime)
each tick: run the biggest task, park it; release tasks whose cooldown ended
solutions.intuition: Always running the task with the most copies left keeps the busiest task from forcing idle time at the end. A queue holds tasks that are cooling down.
solutions.remember: Run the most frequent ready task; park it for n ticks.

solutions.label: Best
steps: answer = max(total tasks, (maxFreq − 1) × (n + 1) + countOfMax)
solutions.intuition: The busiest task decides the shape: (maxFreq − 1) blocks of length n + 1, plus a final row for every task tied at maxFreq. If there are more tasks than slots, no idle time is needed at all.
solutions.remember: max(tasks, (maxFreq − 1)(n + 1) + countOfMax).

problems.title: Find Median from Data Stream
problems.story: Two sand piles: the left pile is a MAX-heap (small half), the right pile a MIN-heap (big half). Keep them the same size and the median sits on top.
problems.statement: Design a structure that takes numbers one at a time and returns the current median at any moment.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: keep a sorted vector; insert at upper_bound

solutions.label: Best
steps: push to lo (max-heap), move lo.top to hi (min-heap)
if hi bigger, move hi.top back to lo
solutions.intuition: The median sits between the smaller half and the larger half. Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, balanced in size, so the median is always on top.
solutions.remember: Two heaps: max-heap small half, min-heap big half.

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.story: Delivery slots on a timeline: sort by start time. If the next slot starts before the current one ends, just stretch the current one.
problems.statement: Merge all overlapping intervals.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: keep merging any overlapping pair until no pair overlaps

solutions.label: Best
steps: sort by start
overlap with last merged → extend its end, else append
solutions.intuition: After sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the one just before it in the merged list. So either extend the last merged interval or start a new one.
solutions.remember: Sort by start; overlap → stretch the end.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.story: Three zones on the calendar: slots fully BEFORE the new one (copy them), slots that OVERLAP it (swallow them), slots fully AFTER it (copy them).
problems.statement: Insert a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list, merging where needed.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: append the new interval, sort, run Merge Intervals

solutions.label: Best
steps: copy all that end before new starts
swallow all that start before new ends (min start, max end); copy the rest
solutions.intuition: The list is already sorted, so it splits into three runs: intervals entirely before the new one, intervals overlapping it, and intervals after it. Copy, merge, copy.
solutions.remember: Before, overlap (merge), after.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.story: Rooms = delivery riders. A min-heap holds "when does each rider become free". The earliest-free rider is done before the new order starts? Reuse him. Otherwise hire a new rider.
problems.statement: Given meeting times, return the fewest rooms needed so no two meetings in a room overlap.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: at each start time, count intervals covering it; answer = max count

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: sort by start; min-heap of end times
earliest end ≤ start → pop (reuse); push this end; answer = heap size
solutions.intuition: Process meetings by start time. A room is free if the meeting that ends earliest has already finished, so keep end times in a min-heap and reuse that room.
solutions.remember: Min-heap of end times; reuse the earliest-free room.

solutions.label: Best
steps: sort starts and ends separately
sweep: a start → rooms++, any end ≤ that start → rooms−−
solutions.intuition: Only the number of rooms matters, not which one. Sort starts and ends separately and sweep: a start takes a room, an end that happened by then gives one back. The peak is the answer.
solutions.remember: Sweep starts and ends; track the peak.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.story: Greedy party planner: always keep the meeting that ENDS earliest, because it leaves the most room for everyone after it. Count the ones you cancel.
problems.statement: Remove the fewest intervals so the rest do not overlap.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: sort by start; LIS-style DP of the longest non-overlapping chain
answer = n − longest chain

solutions.label: Best
steps: sort by END
start ≥ last kept end → keep it, else remove it
solutions.intuition: To keep as many intervals as possible, always keep the one that ends earliest: it leaves the most room for everything after it. Anything that overlaps the last kept interval is removed.
solutions.remember: Sort by end, keep the earliest finisher.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.story: Fly over the sea with a paint bucket: land on any unpainted land, flood-paint the whole island, count +1. Repeat.
problems.statement: Count the islands in a grid of "1" (land) and "0" (water). Land connects up, down, left and right.

solutions.label: DFS flood fill
steps: scan cells; on '1' → count++, DFS sinks the island to '0'
solutions.intuition: Each unvisited land cell starts a new island. Flood-fill from it to mark the whole island, so it is never counted again.
solutions.remember: New land → count + 1, sink the whole island.

solutions.label: BFS
steps: same idea with a queue (no deep recursion)
solutions.intuition: Same flood fill with a queue instead of recursion, which avoids deep call stacks on large grids. Mark cells when you push them.
solutions.remember: BFS flood fill; mark on push.

solutions.label: Union-Find
steps: every land cell starts as its own island (count++)
union with right/down land neighbours; each successful union → count−−
solutions.intuition: Treat every land cell as its own island, then join neighbouring land cells. Every successful join merges two islands into one, so subtract one per join.
solutions.remember: Islands = land cells − successful unions.

problems.title: Rotting Oranges
problems.story: Multi-source BFS is a rumour spreading: every rotten orange starts gossiping at minute 0, and each minute the rumour moves one ring outward.
problems.statement: Every minute, rotten oranges rot their fresh neighbours. Return the minutes until none are fresh, or −1 if some never rot.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: each minute scan the whole grid, rot fresh neighbours of rotten ones
stop when nothing changes

solutions.label: Best
steps: push ALL rotten cells first, count fresh
BFS level by level = minutes; fresh left → −1
solutions.intuition: All rotten oranges spread at the same time, so start BFS from all of them at once. Each BFS level is one minute; if fresh oranges remain at the end, they were unreachable.
solutions.remember: Multi-source BFS: level = minute.

problems.title: Number of Provinces
problems.story: Friend circles: everybody shakes hands (union) with their direct friends. Count how many separate circles are left standing.
problems.statement: Given a city connection matrix, count the groups of cities that are directly or indirectly connected.

solutions.label: DFS
steps: for each unvisited city: count++, DFS marks its whole province
solutions.intuition: A province is a connected component. Each DFS from an unvisited city marks its whole province, so count how many DFS calls you start.
solutions.remember: Count DFS starts.

solutions.label: Union-Find
steps: start with n components; union every connected pair
each union that merges two roots → components−−
solutions.intuition: Start with every city alone and union each connected pair. Each union that joins two different groups reduces the number of provinces by one.
solutions.remember: n − successful unions.

problems.title: Course Schedule
problems.story: Getting dressed: socks before shoes, shirt before tie. If the rules loop (shoes before socks before shoes), it's impossible. Keep picking clothes that have no pending prerequisites.
problems.statement: Courses come with prerequisites [course, needs]. Can you finish all of them?

solutions.label: DFS cycle check
steps: colours: 0 = new, 1 = on current path, 2 = done
reaching a 1 again = cycle
solutions.intuition: You can finish everything unless the prerequisites form a cycle. In DFS, reaching a node that is still on the current path (grey) means a cycle.
solutions.remember: Grey node seen again → cycle → false.

solutions.label: Kahn's BFS
steps: indegree count; queue all with indegree 0
pop, "take" it, decrement neighbours; taken == n → possible
solutions.intuition: Repeatedly take a course with no remaining prerequisites and remove its edges. If a cycle exists, its courses never reach zero prerequisites, so fewer than n get taken.
solutions.remember: Kahn: take indegree 0, count; count < n → cycle.

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.story: Same as getting dressed, but now write down the ORDER in which you picked clothes off the "no pending prerequisites" pile.
problems.statement: Return an order in which all courses can be taken, or [] if that is impossible.

solutions.label: DFS post-order
steps: DFS with colours; add a node when it finishes
reverse the finish order; a cycle → return {}
solutions.intuition: In DFS a course finishes only after every course that depends on it has finished. Reversing the finish order therefore puts every course before its dependents.
solutions.remember: Reverse post-order = valid order.

solutions.label: Kahn's BFS
steps: queue of indegree-0 nodes; pop order = answer
fewer than n popped → cycle → {}
solutions.intuition: The order in which Kahn's algorithm removes indegree-0 courses is already a valid schedule.
solutions.remember: Kahn's pop order is the answer.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.story: Dijkstra is water flowing through pipes: always flood the NEAREST dry junction next (min-heap by distance). The last junction to get wet is the answer.
problems.statement: A signal starts at node k and travels along timed edges. How long until every node has it? −1 if some never do.

solutions.label: Bellman-Ford
steps: relax every edge V−1 times
any node still ∞ → −1, else max distance
solutions.intuition: A shortest path uses at most n − 1 edges. Relaxing every edge n − 1 times lets distances spread along any such path. The slowest node's distance is the answer.
solutions.remember: Relax all edges n − 1 times.

solutions.label: Dijkstra
steps: min-heap of (dist, node); skip stale entries
relax neighbours: d[u] + w < d[v] → update, push
solutions.intuition: With non-negative times, the closest unfinished node's distance can never improve later. Always finalise the nearest node next with a min-heap, and relax its edges.
solutions.remember: Always expand the nearest node (min-heap).

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.story: Every word is a metro station; changing one letter is one stop. BFS finds the fewest stops. Bidirectional BFS sends two trains from both ends to meet in the middle.
problems.statement: Change one letter at a time, every step a dictionary word. Return the number of words in the shortest chain from begin to end.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: BFS; neighbours = every unused dictionary word that differs by exactly 1 letter

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: BFS; neighbours = try all 26 letters at each position, keep those in the set
erase from set when visited
solutions.intuition: Each word has only L × 26 possible one-letter changes, far fewer than comparing with every word. Generate them and keep the ones in the dictionary; BFS gives the fewest steps.
solutions.remember: Generate neighbours by changing one letter.

solutions.label: Best
steps: two frontiers (from begin and from end); always expand the smaller one
a neighbour found in the other frontier → they met
solutions.intuition: BFS from both ends at once and always expand the smaller frontier. The search space grows much more slowly because two small circles meet before one big circle would.
solutions.remember: Two BFS frontiers meet in the middle.

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.story: Bellman-Ford with a stop budget: run exactly k + 1 rounds of "relax every route", reading only LAST round's prices so no route sneaks in two hops in one round.
problems.statement: Find the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops; −1 if impossible.
problems.example: the graph in the picture, k = 1 → 700

solutions.label: Bellman-Ford (k+1 rounds)
steps: d = ∞, d[src] = 0
k+1 times: nd = copy of d; relax every flight using d; d = nd
solutions.intuition: Round i of Bellman-Ford finds the cheapest prices using at most i flights. Run k + 1 rounds, and read only the previous round's prices so no round uses two flights.
solutions.remember: k + 1 rounds, read from last round's copy.

solutions.label: Dijkstra with stops
steps: heap of (cost, node, edgesUsed); first pop of dst = cheapest
skip if edgesUsed > k or we already reached node with fewer edges
solutions.intuition: Dijkstra by cost, but the state includes how many flights were used. A cheaper path that uses too many flights is skipped, and a city is revisited only if reached with fewer flights.
solutions.remember: Cheapest first, but track flights used.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.story: At every item you reach a fork: TAKE it or SKIP it. n forks → 2ⁿ leaves → 2ⁿ subsets. Or think of n light switches and count in binary.
problems.statement: Return all subsets (the power set) of distinct numbers.

solutions.label: Backtracking
steps: bt(i): at the end, save cur
take nums[i] → bt(i+1) → undo; skip → bt(i+1)
solutions.intuition: Each element is either in the subset or not. Branch on take / skip for every element; the leaves of that tree are all 2ⁿ subsets.
solutions.remember: Take it or skip it.

solutions.label: Cascading
steps: start with {{}}; for each x, copy every existing subset and add x
solutions.intuition: Every subset of the first i + 1 numbers is a subset of the first i numbers, with or without the new number. So copy what you have and add the new number to each copy.
solutions.remember: Copy every subset and add x.

solutions.label: Bitmask
steps: mask from 0 to 2ⁿ−1; bit i set → include nums[i]
solutions.intuition: Number the subsets 0 … 2ⁿ − 1. Bit i of the number says whether nums[i] is included.
solutions.remember: Bit i on → take nums[i].

problems.title: Permutations
problems.story: Musical chairs: try every person in chair 1, then solve the remaining chairs. Swap someone in, recurse, swap them back.
problems.statement: Return every ordering of distinct numbers.

solutions.label: used[] array
steps: pick any unused element, mark used, recurse, unmark
solutions.intuition: Fill positions one by one; each position can take any number not yet used. A used[] array tracks that, and you undo after exploring.
solutions.remember: Pick unused, recurse, unpick.

solutions.label: In-place swaps
steps: position i: swap each j ≥ i into i, recurse on i+1, swap back
solutions.intuition: Position i can be filled by swapping any later element into it. After recursing on the rest, swap back so the array is unchanged for the next choice.
solutions.remember: Swap in, recurse, swap back.

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.story: A coin jar you may reuse: at each coin either use it AGAIN (stay on the same index) or move on to the next coin. Stop as soon as you overshoot.
problems.statement: Return all combinations of candidates (each usable any number of times) that sum to target.

solutions.label: Backtracking
steps: bt(start, remaining): loop i from start
choose c[i] → bt(i, rem − c[i]) (same i = reuse) → undo
solutions.intuition: Stay on the same index to allow reusing a coin, and only move forward to avoid the same combination in a different order.
solutions.remember: Recurse with i (reuse), never go back.

solutions.label: Sorted + pruning
steps: sort first; break the loop as soon as c[i] > remaining
solutions.intuition: Sorted coins let you stop early: once a coin is bigger than what remains, every later coin is too.
solutions.remember: Sorted → break on the first coin that overshoots.

problems.title: Word Search
problems.story: An explorer in a maze with chalk: mark the cell (#) when you step in, try all 4 directions, and wipe the chalk when you back out.
problems.statement: Can the word be traced through neighbouring cells of the board, without reusing a cell?
problems.example: "ABCCED" on the board in the picture → true

solutions.label: Backtracking DFS
steps: from every cell: dfs(i, r, c) matches w[i]
mark, explore 4 neighbours for w[i+1], unmark
solutions.intuition: Try every cell as a start. Mark a cell while it is on the current path so it is not reused, and unmark it when you back out so other paths can use it.
solutions.remember: Mark, explore 4 ways, unmark.

solutions.label: Pruned
solutions.time: same worst case, faster in practice
steps: board lacks enough of some letter → false immediately
start from the rarer end of the word (reverse it if needed)
solutions.intuition: Quick checks cut the search: if the board lacks enough of some letter, stop at once; and starting from the rarer end of the word creates fewer false starts.
solutions.remember: Count check first, start from the rarer end.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.story: To stand on step n you came from step n−1 or n−2. Ways(n) = Ways(n−1) + Ways(n−2). It's Fibonacci wearing sneakers.
problems.statement: You climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many different ways reach step n?

solutions.label: Naive
steps: plain recursion f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2)

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: table dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2]
solutions.intuition: The last move to step n was either 1 or 2 steps, so ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2). Store each value once instead of recomputing it.
solutions.remember: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2).

solutions.label: Best
steps: keep only the last two values
solutions.intuition: Each value only depends on the two before it, so two variables are enough.
solutions.remember: Keep only the last two.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.story: A thief walking down a street: at each house, "rob it + best from two houses back" OR "skip it and keep the best so far".
problems.statement: Rob houses for the largest total without robbing two neighbours.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: go(i) = max(go(i−1), nums[i] + go(i−2))

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: dp[i+2] = max(dp[i+1], dp[i] + nums[i])
solutions.intuition: At each house you either skip it (best so far stays) or rob it (its money + best from two houses back). Store the best for every prefix.
solutions.remember: best[i] = max(skip, rob + best[i − 2]).

solutions.label: Best
steps: two rolling variables prev2, prev1
solutions.intuition: Only the last two best values are needed, so roll them forward in two variables.
solutions.remember: Two rolling variables.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.story: The shopkeeper's notebook: for every amount from 0 to target, write "fewest coins to make this". Each amount = 1 + best of (amount − coin).
problems.statement: Fewest coins (unlimited supply) that make the amount; −1 if impossible.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every coin, recurse on amount − coin, keep the min

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: same recursion + memo[amount]
solutions.intuition: The fewest coins for an amount depends on the fewest coins for (amount − coin). The plain recursion solves the same amounts many times; a memo stores each once.
solutions.remember: Memoise f(amount) = 1 + min f(amount − coin).

solutions.label: Best
steps: bottom-up: dp[0] = 0, dp[a] = min(dp[a − c] + 1)
dp[amount] still "infinite" → −1
solutions.intuition: Fill answers from 0 up to the target, so every smaller amount is ready when you need it.
solutions.remember: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a − coin]), bottom-up.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.story: Patience solitaire: put each card on the leftmost pile whose top is ≥ it (binary search), or start a new pile. The number of piles is the LIS length.
problems.statement: Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: take/skip each element, remembering the previous taken index

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]
solutions.intuition: The longest increasing run ending at i extends the best run ending at some earlier smaller number.
solutions.remember: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] with nums[j] < nums[i].

solutions.label: Best
steps: tails[k] = smallest tail of any increasing run of length k+1
lower_bound x: replace it, or append if x is the biggest
solutions.intuition: For every length keep the smallest possible ending value. A smaller ending is always better because it leaves more room to extend. Each new number replaces the first ending ≥ it (binary search) or extends the list.
solutions.remember: Patience piles: lower_bound and replace.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.story: A 2-D grid of the two words: letters match → step diagonally and add 1; otherwise take the better of "up" or "left".
problems.statement: Length of the longest subsequence that both strings share.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: match → 1 + go(i+1, j+1); else max(go(i+1, j), go(i, j+1))

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: dp[i][j] = match ? dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 : max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1])
solutions.intuition: If the last letters match, they are part of the LCS: 1 + LCS of both prefixes. Otherwise drop the last letter of one string and take the better result. A 2-D table stores each prefix pair once.
solutions.remember: Match → diagonal + 1, else max(up, left).

solutions.label: Best
steps: one row; keep the old diagonal in a variable
solutions.intuition: Each row only reads the row above, so keep one row and remember the old diagonal value in a variable.
solutions.remember: One row + a diag variable.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.story: Can the ribbon be cut into dictionary words? dp[i] means "the first i letters can be cut". A cut at j works if dp[j] is true and s[j..i) is a word.
problems.statement: Can the string be split into dictionary words (words may repeat)?

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every prefix that is a word, recurse on the rest

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: dp[0] = true; dp[i] = any j < i with dp[j] && s[j..i) in dict
solutions.intuition: The first i letters can be split if some earlier split point j works and s[j..i) is a word. Store this for every prefix instead of re-solving suffixes.
solutions.remember: dp[i] = some dp[j] && s[j..i) is a word.

solutions.label: Best
steps: same DP, but only look back up to the longest word length L
solutions.intuition: The last word cannot be longer than the longest dictionary word, so only check split points within that distance.
solutions.remember: Only look back L letters.

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.story: A typo-fixing grid with three keyboard moves: insert (from the left), delete (from above), replace (from the diagonal). Matching letters walk the diagonal for free.
problems.statement: Fewest inserts, deletes and replaces that turn word1 into word2.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: match → go(i+1, j+1); else 1 + min(delete, insert, replace)

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: dp[i][j] = match ? diag : 1 + min(up, left, diag)
solutions.intuition: To turn a prefix of word1 into a prefix of word2, the last move was an insert, delete or replace (free if the letters match). Each prefix pair is stored once in a table.
solutions.remember: Same letter → diagonal; else 1 + min(up, left, diagonal).

solutions.label: Best
steps: one row + a diag variable
solutions.intuition: Each row only needs the row above, so keep one row and the old diagonal value.
solutions.remember: One row + a diag variable.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.story: Can a backpack hold EXACTLY half of the total weight? For each item: put it in or leave it out. A bitset is a row of bulbs, and shift-OR lights up every reachable sum at once.
problems.statement: Can the array be split into two groups with equal sums?

solutions.label: Naive
steps: sum odd → false; take/skip recursion towards sum/2

solutions.label: Optimised
steps: dp[j] = can make sum j; loop j downward so each item is used once
solutions.intuition: You need a subset summing to half the total. dp[j] says whether sum j is reachable; adding a number x makes j reachable if j − x was. Loop j downward so each number is used once.
solutions.remember: Reachable sums, loop downward.

solutions.label: Best
steps: bitset b, b[0] = 1; for each x: b |= b << x
solutions.intuition: A bitset stores all reachable sums as bits. Shifting left by x adds x to every reachable sum at once, 64 sums per operation.
solutions.remember: bits |= bits << x.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.story: A fuel gauge: walk forward tracking the farthest point you can reach. If you're ever standing past it, you're stranded.
problems.statement: nums[i] is your longest jump from index i. Can you reach the last index?

solutions.label: Naive
steps: reachable[] array: from every reachable i mark i+1 … i+nums[i]

solutions.label: Best
steps: far = max(far, i + nums[i]); i > far → false
solutions.intuition: You do not need to know how you reach an index, only how far you can reach. Track the farthest reachable index; if you ever stand beyond it, you are stuck.
solutions.remember: Track the farthest reach.

problems.title: Jump Game II
problems.story: BFS in disguise: each "level" is the stretch you can reach with j jumps. When you walk past the edge of the current level, you must take one more jump.
problems.statement: Return the fewest jumps to reach the last index (it is always reachable).

solutions.label: Naive
steps: dp[i] = fewest jumps to reach i; relax i+1 … i+nums[i]

solutions.label: Best
steps: far = farthest reach; at i == end of current level → jumps++, end = far
solutions.intuition: Think of BFS levels: all indices reachable with j jumps form a range. When you walk past the end of the current range you must take another jump, and the new range ends at the farthest reach seen.
solutions.remember: End of the current range → jumps++.

problems.title: Gas Station
problems.story: A road trip: if total gas ≥ total cost, some start works. Whenever your tank goes negative, every station you passed is a bad start, so restart from the next one.
problems.statement: Stations on a circle give gas[i] and cost cost[i] to reach the next one. Return the start that completes the loop, or −1.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: try every start; simulate the full loop

solutions.label: Best
steps: total += diff; tank += diff
tank < 0 → start = i + 1, tank = 0; total < 0 → −1
solutions.intuition: If the total gas is at least the total cost, some start works. If the tank goes negative at station i, no station between the current start and i can be the start, so restart from i + 1.
solutions.remember: Tank negative → restart after this station.

problems.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
problems.story: A dictionary shaped like a tree: every road sign is a letter, and a flag on a house says "a word ends here". startsWith only needs the road to exist; search also needs the flag.
problems.statement: Implement a prefix tree with insert, search and startsWith.

solutions.label: Naive
steps: keep a hash set of words; prefix query scans every word

solutions.label: Best
steps: node = 26 child pointers + end flag
insert creates missing children; search needs end flag; startsWith just needs the path
solutions.intuition: Words that share a prefix share a path from the root, one letter per edge. Lookups take O(word length) no matter how many words are stored; a flag marks where a word ends.
solutions.remember: Shared prefix = shared path; flag = word ends.
